blocks.text: INNNEWS - The value of the exchange is affected by many factors. It's trying to assess whether the three indicators that are most pertinent to the need for Indonesian devisers (government budgets, running transactions and trading scales) are enough to explain the pressure on current Rupiah.

The APBN deficit can increase the need for financing and import. The deficit of the transaction is running to reflect the need for a state's defection against the outside world. Meanwhile, the trade scales affect the supply of devisas through exports and import goods.

To look at the three indicators' relationship with the exchange rate, we use simple statistical analysis with Indonesian data in the 2000 period of 2024. This analysis is not meant to prove a cause-result relationship, but to measure the closeness of each movement by exchange value.

Statistically, APBN deficit shows the most powerful simple correlation to the value of exchange. But when all three variables are analyzed simultaneously, the transaction runs to have the most powerful relative. The findings are consistent with economic theory because the transaction is running to reflect the needs of devisers and the cost of external economies as a whole.

However, those three indicators did not quite explain the entire rupial emission. In 2013, the transaction deficit was approaching 3% PDB, a trading deficit of over 6 billion US dollars, and the deficit APBN is about 2% GDP. Rupiah is actually depreciated about 10% instead of the previous year, and is in the range of Rp10,500 per US dollar.

Until the quarter I 2026, a new transaction deficit reached about 1.1% GDP, the trade balance still recorded surplus, and an APBN deficit targeted about 2.7% PDB. But rupiah has weakened more than 12% than the late 2025 and traded in Rp18.180 per US dollar range.

This shows that all three indicators remain important because they reflect the need for financing and economic devisers, including due to dependency on energy imports. But all three didn't quite explain the pressure on the current route.
There may be other factors involved. Call for example the power of US dollars and global capital currents to risk perception, economic productivity, and belief in the direction of policy.
Global Factor: US Dollar Boiling · Global Voices
The exchange rate always has two sides: the power of the rupiah and the power of the US dollar.

In the last few years, the United States economy has shown more resilience than most of us have estimated. The U.S. financial markets are still able to attract enormous amounts of capital flow. The bond of the U.S. government is still considered one of the most secure assets in the world, while the US stock market continues to be the primary goal of global investment.

As a result, the demand for the assets of the dollar remains high. As long as global investors continue to put their funds on bonds, stocks, and U.S. financial assets, the demand for dollars will remain strong.

At the same time, various alternatives to the domination of the dollar have yet to evolve into credible competitors. BRICS currency deals that have had a great deal of attention yet have been able to rival the depth and liquidity of the US dollar market.
Therefore, part of the Rupiah subjugation was caused by the fundamental decay of Indonesia. Rupiah also faces the currency supported by the largest, deepest, liquiest financial market in the world.
But this external factor also doesn't explain the whole situation. If the power of the dollar is the only cause, then almost all countries will suffer similar pressures. It's not the truth.
Perception and Reality

The exchange rate doesn't just reflect the economic conditions of today. It also reflects the market belief in future economic conditions. Investors buy or sell assets based on what they expect to happen, not just what happened. Therefore, perception is often part of economic reality itself.

When trust is weakened, capital comes out, the demand for dollars increases, and the rupiah is depressed. It then strengthens risk perception. George Soros calls this mutually amplifying process a reflection of reality, and reality forms expectations.

But the market doesn't react to mere perception. In the end, what's judged is the ability of a country to produce growth, to increase productivity, to create more value, and to maintain fictional and financial stability in the long term.

This is where Indonesia faces a more fundamental challenge. Maybe the Indonesian economy isn't as bad as some, but it's not as strong as the only growth rate. Behind a relatively stable growth there is serious structural problem: low productivity, weak innovation, human capital quality is so left behind, bureaucracy is very slow, and institutions are impeding the creation of value plus.

It's not a matter of a year or two, but it's accumulated over a decade. In normal conditions, those weaknesses may not be very visible. But when the pressure increases, the market starts to consider it as a risk assessment.
Or, the economy has been in a position for Fragile: handle with care. When it's forgotten, there's a rift.

In this context the psychological numbers become important. Rp18,000 levels or Rp20,000 per US dollar don't automatically change the fundamental economy in a second. But numbers like that can change market behavior. If investors read it as a sign of increased risk, the pressure on the Rupiah can grow faster than policy response.
What to do?

In the short run, the priority is to maintain fictional stability and reduce pressure on the deviors. It demands budget discipline: reduce consumptive spending, suppress leaks, and prioritize productive spending. When the fiscal space is narrowed down, rendering-seeking and efficiency is no longer just a management issue, it's a threat to economic stability.
Everyone needs to hold back before things get bad. The 1998 monetary crisis left Indonesia behind nearly a generation. Repeating the same mistake will cost much more.

Various efforts of increased acceptance, including Patriot Bonds and tax adjustments, will only be effective if directed to strengthen economic capacity, not simply close short-term funding. If the accumulated funds are used for consumption, market beliefs can worsen. If used for productive investment, the instrument can strengthen policy credibility.

On the monetary side, the Indonesian Bank faces a real trade-off. Higher interest rates can sustain rupiah but suppress growth. Lower interest rates can support the economy, but risk adding pressure to the rupiah and inflation. If the rupiah reversal starts to interfere with inflation expectations and market trust, the stability of exchange value needs to be a greater priority.

Short-term stabilization is just buying time. In the end, the problem is not just why the rupiah is weakened, it's why the market is judging like that. The answer lies not in foreign market values, but in Indonesia's ability to build economic foundations that have been weak: productivity, efficiency, innovation capacity and credible institutions. In the long run, the rupiah value will follow its underlying economic quality.

(Elwin Tobing, Economic Professor, the President of INADATA, Irvine, US; Writing Book of the New World or NEVER) that gives the blueprint the transformative ecosystem of national innovation as a absolute requirement to 2050 Gold Indonesia.)
